variants.name: Askama compile-time templates (#[derive(Template)])
variants.implementation_notes: Askama compiles templates into Rust: annotate a struct with #[derive(Template)] and #[template(path = "orders.html")] (or source = "..."), and the derive reads the template, checks every variable against the struct's fields and generates a Display implementation - escaping is applied unless the |safe filter is used. Choose it when templates ship inside the binary and the compiler should police the marker/model contract.
pitfalls: Templates are compiled into the binary and read at build time: editing one needs a rebuild, and a missing template file is a compile error, not a runtime 500.
The |safe filter turns off escaping for that value, and the escaping is HTML-oriented - a non-HTML template needs its own escaper or pre-escaped content.
Every value the template reads must exist on the struct, so the model has to be assembled completely before rendering.

variants.name: MiniJinja runtime engine (Jinja2 syntax, serde models)
variants.implementation_notes: MiniJinja is the runtime counterpart: create an Environment (optionally with path_loader), add templates from files or strings, and render any serde-serializable value with tmpl.render(context!(...)) - Jinja2 syntax including {% extends %}, {% include %} and macros, with auto-escaping configured per environment. Choose it when templates change without recompiling the binary (plugins, configuration, user-editable reports) or when the compile-time derive pass is unwelcome for a large template set.
pitfalls: Undefined values are lenient by default: a renamed field renders as empty text instead of an error, so switch to the strict behaviour or pin a render test.
Template parse errors surface at load or render time; load templates at startup so a syntax error is a startup failure, not a request failure.
The engine does not sandbox untrusted templates by itself: rendering end-user-supplied templates requires a restricted environment and limits.
